newsitem.title: INDIA: Stay neutral on India oil stocks - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Stay neutral on India oil stocks - analysts.

text.p: An impending increase in government-controlled oil prices has pushed Indian refiner shares higher but analysts now say they are advising caution.
"Be neutral, don't go overweight," said Tridib Pathak, oil analyst at UBS Securities, the investment arm of Union Bank of Switzerland.
An increase in oil prices will not boost profits for oil refiners because their earnings are pegged at a government-set formula of 12 percent post-tax return on employed funds.
A policy-vetting committee of India's 15-party coalition government was meeting on Sunday to find ways to tackle a huge oil subsidy bill.

India imports most of its oil but sells petroleum products to domestic customers below world prices through a complex cross-subsidy system, under which oil refiners are reimbursed their costs from an oil pool account.
The deficit in this account on March 31, 1997, was 155 billion rupees ($4.3 billion).
The sole oil importer, state-owned Indian Oil Corporation (IOC), and other refiners have not been paid their dues.
IOC was the worst hit as it had to borrow funds to pay for imports. The money owed to IOC accounts was about 65 percent of the oil pool deficit, analysts said.
Higher oil prices will help refiners like Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd (HPCL) and Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd (BPCL) improve their cash flows.

UBS's Pathak expects HPCL to report net profit of 5.94 billion rupees for the year ended March 31, 1997 against 5.15 billion a year ago, while BPCL's profit is seen at 4.25 billion rupees against 3.89 billion.
Earnings are forecast to grow at 20 percent over the next year, he said.
"Refiner stocks are the best hedge against oil price increases," said Sanjeev Patni, oil analyst at brokerage W.I. Carr (Far East).
HPCL shares closed at 421 rupees on Friday, up 16.8 percent from 360.50 on March 31. BPCL gained 11.8 percent to 405.75.
Cochin Refineries jumped 35.6 percent to 134.25 rupees after hitting 99 on April 22, while Madras Refineries gained 32.6 percent to 47.75 rupees.
"Oil shares are the best defensive stocks," Pathak said. "They have very secured earnings but I see ample opportunities emerging."

There was no reason for investors to chase stocks because government plans to divest holdings in oil majors -- like IOC, Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC) and Gas Authority of India Ltd (GAIL) -- would increase the supply of oil sector stocks.
Refiners would benefit more if the government began deregulating the tightly-controlled sector but it will not result in runaway profits, Pathak said.
"Deregulation will help companies realise their full earnings capabilities," he said. "Of course there'll be an upside in profits but not huge profits."
